questions.prompt: Which statement best captures what a passing test proves?

options.text: The code is correct for every possible input
The code worked for the specific cases the test tried
The code is faster than the previous version

questions.explanation: Testing shows the presence of bugs, never their absence (Dijkstra). A pass means the tried cases worked — it raises confidence, it does not prove universal correctness.

options.text: Did we build the right product for the user?
Did we build the product right, to its specification?

questions.explanation: Verification = 'did we build it right?' (meets the spec). Validation = 'did we build the right thing?' (solves the real problem).

questions.prompt: Which of these are good reasons a test suite is valuable? Select all that apply.

options.text: It catches regressions when code changes
It encodes the expected behavior so a machine can re-check it
It mathematically proves the program has zero defects
It finds many bugs before users do

questions.explanation: Tests catch regressions, pin expected behavior, and surface bugs early — but they cannot prove the absence of all defects.

questions.prompt: Previously-working behavior that breaks after a later change is called a ____.
questions.explanation: A regression is behavior that used to work and breaks after a change — the classic thing automated tests defend against.

questions.prompt: Order the parts of a single test case as you'd write them.

items.text: Compare the result to the expected value

questions.explanation: A test case sets up inputs, performs the action, then asserts the actual result against the expected result.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The observable wrong behavior at run time
Built the right product (solves the need)

questions.explanation: A defect is the flaw; a failure is what you observe when it runs. Verification checks against the spec; validation checks against the real need.
